speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my appointment as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I have concentrated all my energy to the defence and protection of consumers. It has been a major priority not only for me, but also for the government as a whole. A key element in this battle for consumer rights has been to expose and prosecute cartels and combines. And so it was, for instance, that the fight against sugar companies has taken up part of the efforts of my department in recent years. Hon. members will understand my surprise and disappointment when these companies were recently acquitted by Mr. Justice Mackay.
Following the comments I made on that occasion, Mr. Justice Mackay cited me for contempt of court and a few weeks later, I was found guilty of that charge by Associate Chief Justice Hugessen. Mr. Speaker, I immediately appealed that decision. Both during and after the trial, I refrained from any public statement on that case. Recently, as a result of a clearly calculated indiscretion, my case has given rise to a highly partisan political debate.
It has become quite clear to me in the past few days that my most basic rights, not so much before the courts, but especially before the public at large, as a defendant appealing a decision, could be seriously jeopardized by that political debate, while even my own resolution to keep silent-which goes back to the beginning of my trial-is questioned and used against me by some people. I repeat, I strongly intend to keep that resolution.
I think however that in the case now under appeal, it is not in my interest, as a defendant, nor in the interest of our judicial system that my appeal be heard in an atmosphere of political partisanship which some people, inside and outside the House, have deliberately created. I have no doubt that the Quebec Appeal Court can remain above those political considerations. Still, out of respect for the judicial system, I wish to do what I can to let justice take its course in the best possible climate. I will humbly submit to the decision of the court, whatever it may be, but in the meantime I intend to use every legal recourse that is available to a defendant before the courts.
Secondly, the debate over my case is very likely to jeopardize seriously my efficiency and the value of my work as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Since my appointment, I have applied myself to proving to consumers that I was completely dedicated to their interests. It appears essential to me that consumers should never at any time be left to feel that the Minister responsible for their interests would in any way reduce his efforts on their behalf just to avoid legal or political problems. On the other hand, it seems just as important to
March 16, 1976

me that the minister should never leave himself open to charges of using the interests of consumers as a political screen. There once again, the debates of the last few days and the preposterous comments voiced by some opposition members while listening to me indicate clearly that they intend to make my task very difficult, if not impossible, at least until my appeal has been heard. I believe there are too many things to do, too many urgent tasks to accomplish on behalf of consumers.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that when my case was first brought to court I asked for the advice and counsel of several colleagues and friends, some who are lawyers and some who are not. In particular, I discussed my case with the Minister of Public Works. I emphasize that I appeared before the court pursuant to a summary proceeding. In fact, I was not really opposed by another party; in this case, the court itself was to decide whether I had offended it. I asked the Minister of Public Works whether he could help me, without prejudice to my rights, to determine from Mr. Justice Hugessen what type of apology would be appropriate under the circumstances. I solemnly declare that I have never tried, either directly or indirectly, to exert undue influence on a judge of the Quebec Superior Court, in any case whatsoever, including most definitely the one in which I am involved. Everyone is aware of the integrity and high moral qualities of the Minister of Public Works. I deeply regret that his actions, which he took, in fact only because he is a gracious man, caused him so much embarrassment and unpleasantness which he certainly does not deserve. I want to apologize publicly to him for that.
Both as a citizen now before a court of appeal, and as a minister of the Crown, I cannot properly fulfill the duties I accepted as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Consequently, this morning I tendered my resignation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and he, at my express request, accepted it. I hope that, as an ordinary member of Parliament, my trial will proceed free from all political controversy and I trust that those, in the House as well as outside it, who for their own ends took advantage of these circumstances to carry this matter out of the judicial sphere to make a political football of it, will at least have the common decency to respect my most basic rights.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I assure all Canadians whom I served in the last few years that, as a back bencher, I shall carry on with the same determination the struggles I led as a minister.
With the permission of the House, Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the correspondence exchanged between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and myself. [English]

speechtext: In general terms, because of the importance of the announcement, I might observe that the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) was listened to, in general, with good attention and I think the same ought to apply to the comments by leaders of the opposition parties.

-and to try to pretend that there was some motive here, either partisan or personal in his case, for raising, as I and others in my party have done, questions as to the propriety of his conduct and the conduct of other ministers of the Crown in their relations with the courts. I think it is significant that we should now have an admission that there were conversations between ministers which led to an intervention with a judge who was hearing a case in which the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs was involved. I simply make the point, in passing, that the opportunity to have that kind of conversation with ministers of the Crown, in expectation that an intervention might follow, is a privilege which is not available to the ordinary Canadian involved in processes before the courts of the land.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: The only further comment I wish to make on this point is that since the questioning in this House has led the former minister to the position which he has taken, and has led the Prime Minister, in this case at least, to accept that resignation, and since it has also resulted in an admission by the hon. member for Papineau, the former minister, that there were indeed conversations with other ministers that led to an intervention before the courts in a case in which the minister was involved, we on this side of the House are going to continue to press for a complete and full indication of the nature of the involvement and conversations of the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs with other former and present ministers who might have been involved in what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) has admitted was an intervention in the processes of justice in the land.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in informing the House of his resignation under circumstances that might well have been appropriate for the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) not to castigate members of the opposition for indulging in partisan politics when they were precisely practising their profound obligation as opposition members in a parliamentary system-

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext:
-what the minister's unfortunate need to submit his resignation illustrates today is that the Parliament of Canada can sometimes be effective; because if it had not been for the vigorous pursuit of this issue by members of all parties on this side of the House-not on the other side of the House-I submit to Your Honour we would not have had this resignation today.
The second point I should like to make is that if the hon. member for Papineau has acknowledged that he did a wrong thing in speaking to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) and urging him to intervene on his behalf- because that is what is involved; let us call a spade a spade-and now after all these days he has submitted his resignation, which has been accepted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I ask Your Honour, where does this put the Minister of Public Works? If it is wrong to recommend that someone rob a bank, it is even more clearly wrong, in the context of the law, to carry out that advice. The Minister said in the House yesterday that he accepted responsibility for what he did. I submit that following submission of his resignation and acceptance by the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister himself has some explaining to do in regard to why he can accept one minister's resignation who advised a course of action, but has not accepted another minister's resignation who carried out that advice. We will also continue in our insistence that if the Minister of Public Works does have integrity on this issue, he has an obligation to submit his resignation once again, and that the Prime Minister must accept it.
Let me go back to the need for a public inquiry. If anything, it seems to me that the need for an inquiry is even more apparent today. The Prime Minister has been saying for some days that all the facts are known. That is

strange, Mr. Speaker, because we have just had a new fact presented today that we did not know about. We have had an admission, for the first time, which was not on the public record.
There is a serious issue here in terms of the tradition of parliamentary democracy in Canada. I can think of the Favreau situation in this House some years ago, and there have been others in Great Britain having to do with the importance of cabinet responsibility. How is it that the Prime Minister knows that the course of action taken by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs actually did take place? Did he know some days or weeks ago? If he did, why did he not demand the minister's resignation at that time? If he did not know, then what was the nature of the conversations which took place between the former minister and the Minister of Public Works?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the opposition is not going to be bought off with the kind of sop we were given on Friday. The issue is still as serious as it was. There are almost as many unresolved issues in this matter as there were 24 hours ago, and we shall continue to pursue them.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has resigned because of preceding incidents. Still I think this regretful situation has its good side in that it shows to cabinet members that the judiciary power is one thing and the executive power is another. This shows that a minister, whoever he is, must not interfere in family quarrels whatever the circumstances. Under that aspect, I think that every minister will remain aloof in the future and that this can be taken as a lesson.
As for the allegations that the opposition is playing politics with this issue, Mr. Speaker, I would say that when the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was summoned before the courts, he was then charged with contempt of court by Mr. Justice Mackay. But nevertheless we must be fair. After the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs took action against the sugar companies concerned and charged them under the combines legislation, when the decision of Mr. Justice Mackay was made public, I think that every body in this House, whether Tory, Liberal, NDP or Social Crediter, was quite surprised and disappointed indeed.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: These multinational corporations had indeed been attacked on many occasions, especially by my friends from the NDP, who viewed them as a terrible combine. The Conservatives had the same impression and so did the Liberals and us.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: For my part, Mr. Speaker, even though a judgment has been rendered, if the case is on appeal, as a federal member of parliament I still believe there is a sugar combine in Canada.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext:
That is why yesterday my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) asked the
March 16, 1976

Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) whether a Canadian citizen, a member of parliament or anyone else, in a democratic country as ours, where one may express his feelings, may voice his disappointment about a judgment rendered by any judge across the country.

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. OUELLET-REASONS FOR RESIGNATION

I believe that in the future, in order to avoid all these misunderstandings, it would be wise for a government not to appoint a judge through political channels or for services rendered to a political party but rather to contact directly the bar in order to be sure to have judges safe from influences that can arise here and there.
Anyhow, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) had a lesson; he is no longer minister but member for Papineau. Other ministers might have in the future temptations which they must not succumb to if this situation is not to be repeated in the House of Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address my question to the Minister of Public Works who has so magnanimously over the last ten days accepted the blame for somebody else.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Public Works.
The Associate Chief Justice of the Superior Court, Justice Hugessen, has told the Chief Justice that he had the impression that the minister had called him, as reported, in fact, on page 11779 of Hansard for March 12, 1976. Here is what Mr. Justice Deschenes said, and I quote:
Oral Questions
I rather had the impression that he was attempting, if possible, to head off a confrontation between the executive and judicial branches of government.
Can the minister now reveal to the House exactly what he told Justice Hugessen about this matter and who, within or outside the Cabinet, suggested to him that there might be a confrontation which would affect the integrity and independence of the judiciary?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR. DRURY AND JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question has two parts. Regarding the first one in respect of the confrontation, I think the hon. gentleman would agree that a case before the courts in which the court itself appeared to be one of the parties and a member of the executive being the other, carried out as a full-scale battle based on a possible misunderstanding at the outset, would be an unnecessary confrontation, and any conflict based on this misunderstanding appears to me to be inappropriate and useless. It is the job of a public official to avoid this kind of thing if that can be done, and that is what I was seeking to do.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR. DRURY AND JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR. DRURY AND JUDGE HUGESSEN

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question to the Minister of Public Works relates to the statement given to Chief Justice Deschenes by Associate Chief Justice Hugessen to the effect that, and I quote from page 11779 of Hansard of March 12:
The view which Mr. Drury felt was being expressed in some quarters in Ottawa that the proceedings against Mr. Ouellet were in some way a ganging up of the English speaking establishment against prominently placed French speaking persons.
My question to the minister is, was he personally of the opinion that the case against the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was, in fact, a ganging up of the English-speaking establishment against French-speaking ministers?
As to the particular nature of the words used, I think perhaps the paraphrasing which Mr. Justice Hugessen has provided to his superior, the Chief Justice of Quebec, more adequately says what I had to say to him than perhaps anything I could add here.

APPOINTMENT OF CROWN COUNSEL FOR APPEAL OF CONSUMER MINISTER'S CONTEMPT CONVICTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice. In the matter of the upcoming appeal from Mr. Juctice Hugessen's conviction of the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, is the minister satisfied from a monitoring point of view that adequate arrangements have been made for the upholding and defending of Mr. Justice Hugessen's decision, since following the departure of the original counsel appointed the mandate of his replacement appears to have been circumscribed so that his only role may be to provide information that the appeal court requires, rather than being empowered to act as a vigorous advocate on behalf of the Crown, in the same way as counsel for the former minister will undoubtedly and properly act in attempting to overrule Justice Hugessen's decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CROWN COUNSEL FOR APPEAL OF CONSUMER MINISTER'S CONTEMPT CONVICTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the hon. member means by a "monitoring" position of the proceedings. The proceedings by way of contempt are clearly within the area of administration of justice under the jurisdiction of the Attorney General of Quebec, who has appointed in the case the Batonnier of the Quebec Bar, and I am sure the matter is in good hands.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CROWN COUNSEL FOR APPEAL OF CONSUMER MINISTER'S CONTEMPT CONVICTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the sensitivity of the issue of the involvement of the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs with the courts, which the Prime Minister admitted yesterday caused him to consider the possibility of a confrontation between the executive and judicial branches of government, does the Minister of Justice not consider that the utmost care should be taken so that the appeal of the former minister may never be perceived to have been handled in any way other than with the fullest opportunity for both sides to proceed with the utmost vigour to an ultimate conclusion according to the precepts and procedures of justice? Would he not agree that any possible procedural anomalies or handicaps which would appear to favour the appellant would be most undesirable in principle?

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S VIEW OF ECONOMIC CRISIS AND EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance.
It has been reported in the newspapers that an economist for Crang & Ostiguy in Montreal implied a couple of days ago that Canadians so far have only felt the tip of the iceberg with regard to the economic crisis which has hit industrialized countries starting in 1974. Only during the coming two or three quarters will they really be hit right on by restrictions, unemployment and inflation which will continue to be severe. Does the minister believe that the economic crisis will grow during the next six or nine months? Also, does he think that increases in the interest rates, either by the Bank of Canada or the Canadian banking system, will help stamp out or effectively fight inflation, or will not the opposite happen?

subsubtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER REFUSED MR. DRURY'S RESIGNATION AND ACCEPTED MR. OUELLET'S
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems the question did not cross the minds of many people. I am surprised that the opposition itself did not ask it. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
That in view of the grievous damage the Prime Minister has done to the Canadian democratic system by refusing to accept the resignation of the Minister of Public Works, by not insisting on a full statement to the House by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and by failing to set up an independent inquiry into alleged interference in the course of justice by cabinet ministers, this House declares that the present government does not possess the confidence of the House or the country.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the last two weeks in the House of Commons have not been a pleasant experience for people or for members on either side of the House with any degree of sensitivity. Speaking for myself, I went into politics primarily to devote whatever energy and talents I may have to the question of the redistribution of power and income in Canada, which I take to be the principal concern of my political party.
It has not been pleasant to get involved in what is essentially a moral issue. What is at stake in the motion being moved today is the moral character of the present government. That is something that I, my colleagues and the official opposition, have been calling into question for some days now. During the past two weeks the government has revealed itself to be both dishonourable and arrogant in its actions. Three ministers of the Crown have had their

March 16, 1976
Alleged Interference with Judiciary behaviour described as either improper or grave by judges on the bench of Canada.
The former minister of consumer and corporate affairs has been deeply involved in the whole question at issue. Until today, and in fact including today, he has had neither the forthrightness nor the sense of propriety to make a statement which clearly acknowledges his own wrongdoing. He hid, and hid falsely, in the past two weeks behind a legalism which no lawyer on either side of the House would support, instead of coming clean about his role in the procedures and steps that led to the submission of a resignation by a minister, even though it was quickly rejected by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Even today, when the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) got to his feet to submit his resignation, we did not get, as the sequence of events unfolded, an admission of his own culpability.
Later in the question period, the Prime Minister answered a question from a Liberal backbencher as to the reason for the resignation. There was no acknowledgement in the letter of resignation from the hon. member for Papineau, the letter to which the Prime Minister referred, that he was guilty of some wrongdoing. The reason the minister gave this afternoon for resigning is simply incredible. Essentially what he said was that he could not carry out his ministerial responsibilities while another case in which he is involved was proceeding through the courts. I say, again, that is an absurd reason. The only reason for resigning is the one he should have given, namely, of wrongdoing in the first place. I will come to that in a few minutes.
To complete the week, as if it were not bad enough, in which we had this description of wrongdoing by three and, indeed, four ministers, we had the Prime Minister make what I thought was the most disreputable decision of his political life last Friday. In a serious perversion of the principles of parliamentary democracy without parallel in our country or in any other parliamentary system, he refused to accept the resignation of a minister whose involvement in the judicial process was seen by everyone, including the minister, as being wrong, unacceptable and unworthy of a member of a Canadian cabinet. In so doing, the Prime Minister revealed in the most glaring fashion that he has no real understanding either of democracy or of the spirit of the rule of law.
The right hon. gentleman sees our country as being ruled by a family or gentlemen's club of which he is the titular head. While it is appropriate for all other Canadians to obey the law, he and his ministers need not do so. The law of the constitution is to be obeyed or ignored, depending on the convenience of the Prime Minister and depending in part also on whether the violators are caught. If they are caught, as members of the club or family, the Prime Minister will accept their apologies, gently admonish them and carry on as if nothing of significance had happened. If members of the opposition have the audacity to raise questions about this process, the Prime Minister has the fatuous gall to suggest that we in the opposition are wrong for pursuing such a course.
The state is not a family. Those who make the law in a democratic state must themselves be subject to its laws and constitution. This is precisely what the Prime Minister fails to understand, as his casual and foolish retention of

the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) makes clear. The Prime Minister, I say with some sadness, but seriously, is an elitist who had the misfortune of being born in a democratic age. But his undemocratic behaviour must stop, or be stopped by members of the House of Commons.

I am a Liberal but for the sake of representative government in this country I believe the government must fall for its flagrant abuses of the parliamentary system and the trust the people once placed in them.
That is from a Liberal. I think it sums up the attitude of people from one coast to the other who have been revolted by the course of action taken by the government in recent days.
I want to say something about two of the individual cases involved and why we think there are important, unresolved questions with which only a public inquiry can deal. First, the situation involving the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). As we know-and this is beyond dispute-the minister went to see Mr. Justice Mackay concerning a trial in process in which the defendants were students who had taken part in a disturbance at Sir George Williams University. Here is what Mr. Justice Mackay said in the course of a letter submitted to the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec: he said the minister "felt the situation was so serious that it was decided to see me with a view to delaying the jury's decision." Judge Mackay continues:
I was inwardly disturbed by this visit. Not only did I feel I was being asked to see that the jury's decision was delayed, but if for any reason the defence attorneys learned of the visit there was a possibility of a mistrial after an arduous and expensive eight-week trial.
Mr. Speaker, as clearly as the English language could make any point, if what Judge Mackay tells us actually took place, what happened on that occasion was an attempt to interfere with the judicial process by exercising influence. It is important to note that in Judge Deschenes' report to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) he does not pass judgment on this particular case in one way or another, as he did on other aspects of his report with reference to other ministers involved. He lets the facts speak for themselves. The minister involved has stated in the House on a number of occasions, more particularly last Friday, that what Judge Mackay says is not the case. He has told us that the purpose of seeing the judge was not to influence, alter or change judicial behaviour with regard to a case which was in process, but simply to ascertain information concerning a date in the proceedings.
What are the issues which are unresolved? I submit the incident cannot be dismissed as something which took place years ago and which ought, therefore, to be left in the dustbin of history. There are many present implications arising from this situation, questions which come to mind and which must be settled. First, either Judge Mackay or the Minister of National Health and Welfare is providing us, to resort to a euphemism, with some misinformation. To
March 16, 1976

put it more bluntly, either the judge is lying or the minister is lying. Neither man's statement can be seen as resulting from some slight lapse of memory. Such a suggestion cannot be taken seriously.
How are we to get to the truth of this matter? The Prime Minister has been telling us we are in possession of all the facts. That is absurd, if only because some more facts came out today. One of the advantages of an inquiry would be precisely the advantage which comes from cross-examination to find out who was misinforming whom. If it is the Minister of National Health and Welfare who has been misinforming us, he should go from the cabinet forthwith. If, on the other hand, Judge Mackay is lying, he should be removed from the bench. I will put it as bluntly as that.

speechtext:
I should like to remind the Prime Minister that early in the 1960s, in Great Britain, in the Profumo case, when Mr. Profumo, then minister of war, resigned from the Macmillan cabinet he did so-I recall this because I happened to be there-not because of an indiscretion with a prostitute, but because he was caught lying to the House of Commons and to fellow members of the cabinet. As soon as that became known, Mr. Macmillan made it clear to him forthwith that his resignation was expected. The resignation came, and was promptly accepted. Mr. Profumo took the honourable course of action in offering it, and so did the prime minister in demanding and accepting it. So the Lalonde case, if I may call it that, is important because it has .everything to do, not simply with past behaviour but with the present integrity of members of the cabinet. This integrity must be maintained whatever partisan differences exist in the House of Commons. There must be complete faith in the honesty of members of the cabinet.
The second case about which I want to say something is the case involving the Minister of Public Works. We know that Judge Hugessen was considering the appeal of the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs who was facing a charge of contempt. We know, and this is on the record, that the Minister of Public Works telephoned Judge Hugessen to discuss two points: first, to determine whether an apology would bring proceedings to an end and, second, to inform the judge that some in Ottawa were saying there was an English-speaking establishment gang-up taking place in opposition to French-Canadian ministers, more particularly Mr. Ouellet.
Alleged Interference with Judiciary
Concerning the point as to ganging-up, Judge Hugessen reports-I am choosing the words with care, and quoting them-that he thought the point "ridiculous" and that he "could not even consider" such matters. Judge Hugessen went on to say that in his opinion the Minister of Public Works was trying to "head off a confrontation between the executive and the judicial branches of government." It is also true to say that at the conclusion of his report, Judge Hugessen stated, "I did not think he was attempting to influence my judgment." With all due respect to Judge Hugessen-and of course I am not questioning his integrity on this point-I am going to say something about his judgment and use of language.
The Minister of Public Works got in touch with the judge and made certain claims to which the judge responded. One word he used was "ridiculous"; a second phrase was that "he could not even consider"; and further on he said that the purpose of the conversation was to "head off a confrontation between the executive and the judicial branches of government".
I submit that if the English language means anything, the only purpose that the Minister of Public Works would have in making that phone call was to influence the judge. That is precisely what we mean when we use the word "influence". I checked the meaning of that word in the Oxford dictionary, and the definition is "to have an effect upon". What other purpose would there be in making a phone call to convey that kind of information, if the caller did not intend to influence the judge? I repeat, that is my clear judgment of what was involved. Because this was the unequivocal purpose of what is the normal use of that language, I submit that the course of action taken by the Minister of Public Works was wrong, wrong, wrong, that he should resubmit his resignation and that it should be accepted by the Prime Minister.
I should now like to turn to the case of the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs. If there were ever gradations of wrongdoing among the five people involved in the past week, he must be near the top. He sat there silently over the past two weeks, systematically refusing to answer questions, when for a good part of the time another minister was in one sense taking the blame for a certain course of action. Today the minister rose in this House and announced his resignation. I have a tendency to be naive at times, Mr. Speaker, but we cannot go through another phony routine of the sort we had last Friday. Surely the minister is going to get up and say that he did something wrong, as a result of which he is submitting his resignation.
I listened to the minister with care, but he did not once say he had done something wrong. When the Prime Minister replied to the question of a Liberal backbencher later on, the Prime Minister did not say that the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs had done something wrong. Not at all. What the former minister said was that he needs to be relieved of his ministerial duties so he can fight his present court battle.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is that the acknowledgement of cabinet responsibility? Is that the demonstrable kind of moral leadership that we expect on questions of integrity?

March 16, 1976
Alleged Interference with Judiciary I am not talking about economic policy. Even as late as today the minister does not see that he has done something wrong. He gets to his feet today and says, "Yes, I spoke to the Minister of Public Works and I did urge him to go to the judge and present him with some information. If I give an apology does that mean I will be let off?" In effect, that is what he said. Having stated that, he does not acknowledge it is wrong. This is what this whole debate is about, in a sense. The minister does not recognize today that what he did was wrong, just as the Prime Minister and his colleagues over the past two weeks have not recognized the impropriety of such behaviour.
I have no doubt of the scenario that is in the mind of the Prime Minister, and it is this. Once the court proceedings are finished in the hon. member for Papineau's case, the Prime Minister will trot out his letter of resignation and say, "You see, his resignation had nothing to do with interference with the judicial process; oh no, God forbid. The reason he resigned was to fight his case. Now his case is over, of course, we can take him back in the ministry". I predict that that course of events has likely already occurred to the Prime Minister, just as the sequence of last Friday, where one minister submits his resignation in the morning and it is withdrawn in the afternoon, had probably been worked out the previous Thursday night.
There are a number of very serious questions that remain unanswered, Mr. Speaker. Did the hon. member for Papineau tell the Prime Minister about his involvement with the Minister of Public Works? Did he, in the past two weeks, go to him and say, "Yes, I urged him to have the conversation with the judge", which he described here today? If he did, we never knew it from the Prime Minister. He kept telling us that he had all the facts, but he did not take the trouble to give them to us. All he said, with great care was, "I have listened to both sides and I have decided there was no wrongdoing".
If the Prime Minister heard from the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs, and he then went to the Minister of Public Works to urge him to intervene with the judge, then I seriously submit that the Prime Minister himself has been derelict in his responsibility as Prime Minister of this country. We want to know about those conversations, about what the Prime Minister knew about the case, and when he was told. We want to know what conversations took place between the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Papineau. Yet we have all this talk of cabinet solidarity, supported by backbenchers who don't have one ounce of the courage of the backbenchers of Great Britain in both Labour and Conservative parties who would have revolted weeks ago over an issue like this.

speechtext:
Let me remind howling Liberal backbenchers that a man named Favreau resigned from this House not that long ago. The reason for his resignation is also important. The reason he submitted his resignation was that he had misinformed his Prime Minister. We want to know how many ministers on that side may well have misinformed their Prime Minister on this issue. If the Prime Minister has been misinformed by those ministers,

they should be out of the cabinet. If, in turn, he has been told the truth, then he should resign as Prime Minister.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I said at the outset that the government's action during the past two weeks has been dishonourable, and I repeat that. The Prime Minister and his government have done a profound disservice to parliamentary democracy in our country. Ministers have abrogated their serious obligation to keep distinct the judicial and executive functions of government in our country. By not reacting swiftly to obtain or accept resignations in such a situation, the Prime Minister himself has abused the responsibility of his office. By treating such conduct by ministers as a mere breach of good conduct among gentlemen in a club, the Prime Minister has trivialized, in a cynical way, constitutional law and practice in our country, and I say in all seriousness that he has fed the forces already loose in our country that promote disregard of the law.
By not having insisted that the role played in this affair by the minister of consumer and corporate affairs and by others be fully aired, the Prime Minister has left himself and our institutions open to the serious charge of a cover-up. The integrity of the Prime Minister's office itself is open to challenge on this issue. This, Mr. Speaker, constitutes, I submit, a great disservice to the people of our land.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit I feel very honoured today. I thought I was being mistaken for the leader of the official opposition. I am not too sure what happened but anyway I am pleased I have been given the floor. Mr. Speaker, I think the NDP members are trying to correct the mistake they made yesterday when they moved for adjourment simply to stop working
March 16, 1976

and go and doze in their offices. We are here to work and we proved it yesterday, that is why we voted against their motion.
Today, the motion tabled before the House includes three issues within one problem concerning the independence of our judiciary system. I shall attempt to refer to all three briefly.
The mover states:
That in the view of the grievous damage the Prime Minister has done to the Canadian democratic system by refusing to accept the resignation of the Minister of Public Works ...
-that the government can no longer have the confidence of the House following the questions of privilege raised on March 12, 1976 by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury), when the first expressed his regrets to Mr. Justice Aronovitch, the second also did so to Mr. Justice MacKay and the third one gave us a frank explanation, and even indicated he was glad that Mr. Justice Hugessen said that, in his view, the Minister of Public Works did not attempt to influence his judgment in the case of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
After professing his belief in the independence of the judiciary, the Minister of Public Works (M. Drury) said that he was in complete agreement with the Associate Chief Justice and stated impressively in the House, and I quote:
I very much regret taking the action which I did and which the Associate Chief Justice has characterized as improper, and for this I sincerely and deeply apologize to all those affected. I have, accordingly, tendered to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) my resignation from the ministry.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the action of a gentleman who recognized his mistakes and did the only thing he could do. Everyone in this House respected the gesture of the Minister of Public Works and was glad to end all these discussions which do not contribute to the effective running of the business of the House. I have always thought that by so acting for the greater interest of Canadian justice, the resigning minister, far from humiliating himself, drew the admiration of the Canadian people. Indeed, when I spoke after his resignation, I spoke with the greatest of sincerity, Mr. Speaker, and said this:
Mr. Speaker, I think the event which concerns us this morning must be a landmark in the judicial history of our country. And I hope that after all the events of the last few days, today's discussions and actions will result in a warranty of the integrity of our judicial system all over Canada.
This morning, we heard excuses from various ministers... This morning, we accept, not lightheartedly, the resignation of a minister. He is one of the ministers I admired most in the House for his honesty and integrity. This probably shows that we the people-I want to be the people's voice-see that the function of minister is not always a sinecure, that this function brings some responsibilities. Above all, the ministers being surrounded as they are by people who constantly clamour for more, I can understand that they, or hon. members, might be tempted to try and give more help to those around them who exert pressures ceaselessly. That is how I see the work the minister did with the judge, and I congratulate him for his action this morning: it is a guarantee for Canada that, among parliamentarians, there are still people who can recognize that they may have gone too far, who can go back and bow before the requirements of public interest.
I shall stop here, Mr. Speaker, and simply say that following this resignation that everyone accepted and after
Alleged Interference with Judiciary learning through the newspapers that the right hon. Prime Minister had a long talk with the Minister of Public Works before he made his statement, I was convinced there had been agreement on what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) did. Had that meeting not given positive results, there was no point then in the Minister of Public Works tendering his resignation. If he knew in advance that it would not be accepted, why tender it? Did they want to give a show in this House and mock the people?
I confess quite sincerely, Mr. Speaker, that I was astounded when I heard the right hon. Prime Minister say he did not accept the resignation of the Minister of Public Works. I had so much confidence in the sincerity of the resigning minister that I thought he would rise immediately in the manner of the good military man he was and state to the Prime Minister that his decision was beyond appeal. But nothing of the kind happened, and there is this impression that everything was well orchestrated in advance to give more zest to the statements.
And what does the people think about all that? That it has to pay the piper again and that our justice will continue to be under the influence of all political currents. The various governments will continue to appoint judges of their choice who are highly regarded in the party or have served the party well.
After all that attempts will still be made to convince the people that our judicial system is safe from any political influence. What is urgently needed is a reform of our judicial system so those political appointments will stop once and for all.
As to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), I will be brief because his case dates back several years when he was not even a minister. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I never dig out the dead. My function is to bury them well.
If the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs did what he had to do this afternoon it is because he accepts to free justice and at the same time, hopefully, perhaps speed up the fight undertaken against the cartels that control our Canadian economy.
I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that as far as Mr. Justice Mackay is concerned, I cannot but share the views of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). Incidentally, all the people I have met are unanimous in saying that the three sugar companies constitute one of the most dangerous trust ever against consumers, who were obliged to pay appalling prices for sugar. When will this government stop protecting all these trusts which determine our living conditions and are primarily responsible for the inflation we have been facing for the past few years?
The working people are again punished because of inflation, whereas all these trusts of every description can operate freely and make substantial profits every month.
Mr. Speaker, the motion also refers to setting up an inquiry. As regards the setting up of an independent inquiry into interference by a cabinet minister, I suggest, when all players have left the arena, that it will be useless to spend millions of dollars on analyzing a debate that will be completed, but this is on the clear understanding that the

In this whole business, the Prime Minister deliberately used a diversion tactic, by refusing, basing himself on false premises, to direct a public inquiry. This statement, among others things, brings two facts to light: first, Mr. Justice Deschenes did not conclude that there was no attempt to influence the normal course of justice; in fact, the Chief Justice clearly said that he neither could nor would judge the conduct of the Minister of Public Works. All he did was exonerate his own court; second, the Associate Chief of Justice could only say that he had not been influenced and that he could not judge Mr. Justice Mackay's allegations because he had not been aware of the conversations between the two ministers. [English]
In refusing a serious and full investigation yesterday into these matters, the Prime Minister said:
In so far as investigation of the facts, we believe that the facts which have to be known, in so far as they might or might not have consisted of contempt of court or interference with justice have now been made known by the courts.
The Prime Minister might believe, or might pretend to believe, that these are the only facts that need to be known. We need to know the full facts about any conversations between representatives of the Prime Minister and the judge hearing the case involving students from Trinidad, and we need to know any other facts which may be relevant. Mr. Speaker, the motion of no confidence criticizes me, the Prime Minister, on three grounds. I shall deal with the three in turn. The first is that I refused the resignation of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury). Mr. Speaker, very briefly I should like to remind the House of the origin of this matter. It originated in contempt proceedings which are of a special kind. There are two mechanisms for proceeding in contempt proceedings. One is by way of indictment or accusation where there are two parties, the Crown on one side and the accused on the other, each with their lawyer, and the judge in a criminal case who tries to judge between the Crown and the accused-the accused always, under our system, having the benefit of the doubt-and trying to reach the fairest and most equitable judgment.
The other procedure, which is less and less used in democratic countries, is where the judge or the courts judge, themselves, whether they have been offended or not. There are no two parties, the Crown and the accused, but the courts are sitting in judgment to determine whether they have been interfered with or otherwise outraged or influenced. In this case, the second course was taken.
It is important to remember that the time-honoured avenue of answering this kind of accusation is to make a proper apology, the kind of apology which would be acceptable to the courts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
In the particular procedure which was chosen, it was necessary, therefore, to ask the courts themselves. I am not saying the procedure was right. I did
March 16, 1976

criticize the minister for having used the procedure. But I am going back to the origins of this so that the House and the country understand that in this particular contempt proceeding, the courts were sitting in judgment on whether they had been offended, and it was in some way important to get to know from the courts how, and what, kind of apology they would accept.
This having been established, I said in my statement on Friday that there were different interpretations, in different jurisdictions and in different circumstances, on the question of how do you approach the courts in such circumstances. I laid out those rules in brief form, in summary form, on Friday so that in the future these rules be known and that they be part of the code of conduct of this and, I hope, future governments. I will not deal with that at any length because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Bas-ford), whose proper duty it is, will explain those rules at greater length, and I think the statement of them in an unambiguous way is important so that in future such cases, and any others, people in the government know how to address themselves to the courts.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the essential judgment which remains is that there was improper conduct by the Minister of Public Works in this case. It should be noted that it was not illegal conduct; that it was not complained of by the judge at the time. It was not regarded by that judge as an attempt to influence his judgment. It was not found by the judge or, for that matter, by the Chief Justice, to constitute an interference with the judicial process. Actually, the law officers of the Crown stated that in their opinion there was no such offence. The Minister of Justice will talk about this later. This improper action, this impropriety, was not undertaken for reasons of personal advantage. On the contrary, Mr. Justice Hugessen felt that it was done for the best of motives. He went on to say what he believed those motives were.
The House will remember that I did not condone this action. I even said that I regard it as a serious lapse of judgment. So the question before the House and the question before me is, what should the minister's punishment be for that lapse of judgment, for that improper act? That is the judgment I must make. It is a judgment for which I am accountable to this House. I am speaking to this motion in proper fashion. Incidentally, I am told that I am speaking in my normal turn, as is customary for government members who answer on opposition days. As I say, it is a judgment for which I am accountable. It is one which-I say this without pretension-keeps in mind the best interests of justice and of the country.
On the one hand we have to consider the importance of preserving parliamentary institutions and judicial institutions intact and making sure, to use the words of some commentators, that they are not brought into opprobrium through misconduct. On the other hand we have to consider the reputation and future career of a devoted and honourable public servant.

I said that an inquiry, by definition, the very meaning of the word, pertains to inquisitorial forms of justice where you do not presume people are innocent but where you presume there is some guilt somewhere and you start asking questions of the people whom you suspect might be guilty of wrongdoing. As I said the other day, this type of fishing expedition is either to satisfy the ambition or aspirations of some or perhaps to satisfy the pique or curiosity of others. However, I say that they are contrary to the fundamental concepts of the rule of law. They are anathema to anyone who truly believes in individual rights and principles.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Such fishing expeditions, such inquiries- I have explained this many times in the House when refusing this request which has been made repeatedly by the opposition-are to my mind only justifiable when the normal judicial procedure cannot be followed, when there are reasonable and probable grounds to believe that the full facts are not known and cannot be known through the normal judicial process or, I would add, in the case of parliament, through normal parliamentary processes. That is why, under our system, if a member of the public wishes to lay an information and press a charge, that is his right. If a member of the opposition wishes to do that, well, that is fine, too, and the procedures are provided. But suspicion, innuendo, calumny-these are not the bases for proceeding.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The opposition keeps repeating that an inquiry is needed to find out whether there are any further facts, facts which need to be known. Let us look at the three areas of fact which are of interest in this case. Concerning what took place between ministers and judges, we have what the ministers stated in this House last Friday, what they have stated in answer to repeated questions. I have always said that until we had Justice Des-chenes' report-I have heard the ministers and I take their word, but in fairness we must learn whether the courts feel
Alleged Interference with Judiciary aggrieved. That was the object of the letter which the Minister of Justice sent to Mr. Justice Deschenes. In that report, which was made public, we have the version of the three judges. So these facts are known-what the ministers said to the judges and what the judges felt they said when they were spoken to. It is hard to see how any inquiry could ascertain anything more than that. Perhaps there are some slight variations which I am prepared to ascribe to lapses of memory, but if members opposite do not believe this to be the case, if they do not want to take the word of members of parliament, they know what recourse they have.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Only one word more on this aspect-I hate to go even this far, but I have been under questioning in the House-indicating there are some reasons to cast doubt, for instance, on the memory of Mr. Justice Mackay. I have given examples, and it seems to me that if there are fair-minded persons looking at this issue they would at least have an equal cause to suspect his memory as they have that of the minister. When that set of facts is known, there remains-before I gallop to an end-two other sets of facts which might interest the opposition. The first concerns what a minister might have said to another minister. I have said before, and I repeat it now, that the privacy of conversations between any two individuals in society, even if they are ministers, should be respected except when the greater good of society demands otherwise.

speechtext: A lot of claptrap!

I hope I have the agreement of the other side on that principle. They might argue about the circumstances; they might say that in this particular case the good of society demands that we infringe the privacy of conservations. If there was an illegality involved, if there was a conspiracy involved, I would have no doubt that the importance of dealing with that situation was greater than the need to respect the confidentiality of the conservations. We know, now, that there are no such allegations of illegality or of interference with the conduct of justice. We know there has been an impropriety.
Opposition leaders have made a good deal of such questions as this: Did you know about these things beforehand, or not? If you did, why didn't you act? If you didn't, why did you not find out?
Let me say, with regard to this and some of the other innuendoes which have been made, so that ministers may know it, so that members on this side of the House may know it and so members of the opposition may know it, that what two members of my cabinet say to each other is none of my business.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I say parliament also has that right. That is why until Chief Justice Deschenes had looked into this matter and established that the facts were grave and that they had resulted in an impropriety, I refrained from asking in any great detail or with perseverance what the ministers had said to each other. I wanted to know whether they had committed an illegal act, and to that extent I did question them. Until the judgment had been made that there was an impropriety, and until I had this objective version of the judges, I did not press the ministers on every detail that might have gone on in their conversations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: You still find it satisfactory?

speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not find it satisfactory, to answer the leader of the opposition. That is why I got an apology, and the House got an apology, from the minister. speechtext: What facts did the minister withhold from you?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: As far as the minister of consumer and corporate affairs is concerned, he did tell me yesterday the exact nature of his conversations with the Minister of Public Works. Whether that kind of impropriety-advising an impropriety, or asking an impropriety, or whatever the minister said this afternoon he said to the minister-calls for resignation or not, I think is an academic question, since in any event he resigned for other reasons and is no longer a minister of my cabinet. I hope the opposition will also have the decency to do the same.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
In an effort-probably fruitless, but nonetheless an effort-to dispel the suspicions of hon. members opposite, and in an effort to bring parliament back to a more efficient management of the business of the nation, I believe the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs went to the outer limits of what is permissible in regard to what he could say without infringing the sub judice rule. But this is for his judgment, Mr. Speaker; I just feel that he did it at considerable cost to himself, that he did it in a way that will permit him to exercise his right of appeal in this case. In the interim, I believe hon. members should at least respect the price he has paid in order to exercise that right. In the case of the hon. member for Papineau, I submit it is a question either of taking his word that that is what he said and did, or not taking his word and laying a charge in the customary fashion, with the customary consequences, Mr. Speaker.
I have dealt with conversations between ministers and the courts and between one minister and another minister, but it seems to me that there is a third area of uncertainty and that is what one judge might have said to another judge or what judges might have said to their counsel. Of these facts we know little. I am certain that an inquiry could attempt to find out more about that, but I am not sure whether it would be appropriate or desirable for the institution of parliament or the courts to get into that side of the inquiry.
Moreover, I would ask parliament by what mechanism it would conduct that aspect of the inquiry. How would parliament question judges, Mr. Speaker? If they want to question a minister, to cross-examine his version, presumably they would also have to question the judges. How would they do that, Mr. Speaker? There is one known procedure for parliament to question judges, and that is the procedure of impeachment; but I do not think the opposition are suggesting that.

I am very grateful that this fact has been laid to rest once and for all. It seems to me that the

Prime Minister's so-called statement of ethics on Friday is today, on Tuesday, in tatters because of the answers of the Minister of Justice. I look forward to hearing from him later when he will enunciate on this.
The Canadian Bar Association's code of ethics is very clear. I have here the duties of a lawyer in public life. Mr. Justice Deschenes quoted the Quebec Code very clearly. I presume that the Bar Society of the province of Quebec is even now looking into the impropriety of members of the profession in that province as a result of the actions they have taken. The codes of every other province are also very clear in this regard. So really what we have now is no code of ethics.
The Prime Minister has suggested that the sum of our debate here is calumny. He has used the words "calumny" and "innuendo". I say that what we have been doing here, as my leader and the leader of the NDP have suggested, is carrying out the fundamental duty of the opposition in the parliamentary system.
I suggest that for a moment we should turn the whole matter around and ask ourselves what would have happened to the escutcheon of public life in this country if the occurrences of the last couple of weeks had never occurred. There would have been a continuation, presumably, of interventions on the part of ministers with the courts, which is quite contrary to the code of ethics, and there would have been a continuation of what a respected judge has called "grave" and "improper" conduct and for which, on Friday, we had Wynken, Blynken and Nod apologizing to us. But surely it must have been one of the most curious examples of ministerial repentance in my time here. They popped up one after another like popcorn on Saturday night, all apologizing to us and saying that in future they would follow a code which they should have followed long ago.

Hon. members may not think there is a crisis of cynicism, but no less a figure than the Prime Minister of Canada spoke about it over the new year and the problem our institutions face in their public acclaim.
What I have in front of me is not written by the Right Hon. Lester Person, but a magazine edited by Norman Cousins, The Saturday Review of November 1, and it devotes the whole edition to the rather terrifying and unpleasant subject of what is happening to ethical standards in government, law, business, accounting, journalism, medicine, and education.
Because I was smug I did not think such a thing would ever have to be written or that a Canadian magazine would ever have to take up an issue dealing with ethics in our country, but I see; I was as usual, somewhat naive.
In Montreal in the spring of last year many of us were on another mission having to do with this institution, and the mission involved whether democracy itself was governable in the 1970's and 1980's. Government will never be easy, and democracies will never have an easy time of it if there are standards for the executive and standards for the rest of the citizens, and if the rest of the citizens see that the executive is in a different position to the mass of the public. That is what this motion is about, why I welcome it, why I support it, and why I think it behooves every man and woman who represent constituencies in this country to do what they individually can to try to restore faith in our system and to restore an ethical standard to this institution of which we can all be proud. And that has not happened.

speechtext:
I think there are some people in this country, some even in this House, who by their grinning and laughing in the House-I am not talking about the others- show that they totally fail to appreciate the gravity of the matter we are discussing. They do not seem to understand that the independence of the judiciary is a basic pillar of our whole society and our whole system. Failure to understand that and failure to defend it are the basic charge we make against the government on this occasion, and it is a matter which affects the whole fabric and nature of our society.

I should like to read what the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec said in this connection. He said:
It is of the utmost importance that this independence of the judiciary, achieved through great effort during the course of the last three centuries, be jealously guarded against all attacks.
The accusation I have to make is that it is not being jealously guarded. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in particular, through a series of minimizing and downgrading the whole business, has managed to make it look as if it were a trifling matter which does not have to be taken seriously. I have something I want to say later about the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury). I am afraid his conduct also falls in that category. I wanted to speak about him a little later but perhaps I will say what I have to say now.
I have the greatest respect for the Minister of Public Works. It has been one of the greatest disappointments I have ever had that, when he did the honourable thing in this House last Friday, he then permitted the Prime Minister to persuade him to do something less honourable. His first choice was the right choice and I wish he had stuck to it.
How has the Prime Minister downgraded and minimized this thing? One thing he said repeatedly during his speech, not only today but on other occasions, is that there is no illegality here, just an impropriety. He managed to say impropriety as if it did not matter very much. I remind the House that the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec in his report, which appears at page 11779 of Hansard, quotes Associate Chief Justice Hugessen as follows:
While I felt at the time that the call was improper (and I believe I said so to Mr. Drury), I did not think that he was attempting to influence my judgment.
But Mr. Justice Deschenes does clearly refer to the impropriety later when he says:
I have little doubt that the facts related by Mr. Justice Hugessen are grave, considering the stature of the person making the call and the circumstances in which the call was made to him.
I say that we have the judge saying it was a "grave" impropriety, and the Prime Minister tries to brush this aside as though somehow or other the Chief Justice had not taken the matter very seriously. How ridiculous it is to keep on talking about illegality. We all know that if we park in the wrong place that is illegal, and obviously it is not a matter to be taken too seriously by this House. But when you have an interference in the administration of justice such as we have seen clearly and transparently outlined in the facts before the House in the last few days, when you see this sort of thing then the matter is of very grave concern indeed. All the minimizing, brushing aside, use of the word "illegal" as against the word "grave" impropriety-all this is a calculated effort to minimize this and treat it as though it were unimportant, something of no supreme importance.
Another method of attempting to minimize the matter is to talk as though attempting to influence the judiciary was not a critical thing as long as you did not succeed. This is the most ridiculous doctrine that has ever been propounded in parliament at any time, I should think. I am glad that there is not the slightest suggestion that the attempt was
Alleged Interference with Judiciary in any way successful. But the attempt was there; the attempt was highly improper, and deserved to be regarded with full seriousness.
It is absolutely inconceivable-I think the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) has underlined it but it was perfectly clear before-that the Minister of Public Works was sent as his emissary or spokesman or advocate to speak to the judge who was deciding the case of the hon. member for Papineau. If that was not a flagrant example of intervention in the administration of justice I do not know where you would find a clearer case if you had words, and words, and words of evasion. The facts speak clearly for themselves.
I want to read from the report of the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec where he cites a regulation of the bar of Quebec. I am not a member of the bar of Quebec but I presume their regulations are authorized by statute and therefore have the force of law. Regulation 43.3 was cited by the learned judge so he must have thought it relevant. It reads:
In the absence or without the knowledge of the other party or of his advocate, he shall not make, before judgment or decision, on behalf of a party in a contested matter, any verbal or written representations to a judge, a court or the members of a judicial or quasi-judicial body.
I say we do not need any spurious code of ethics thought up by the Prime Minister. This rule sets up a law; it is the law of Quebec and I suggest it is probably the law of other provinces in the country. It is not only the law as written down, it is the law of ordinary morals and ethics. It is the law of the institutions of democracy and ensures their independence. We have seen here an effort to minimize the whole thing.
I did speak of the Minister of Public Works, Mr. Speaker. I repeat that I hold him in respect and I found that one of the most unhappy things that has happened since I have been in this House was that he abandoned his own good judgment and permitted himself to continue to occupy a position which by his actions, however well intentioned, clearly disqualified him from being in the government of this country.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a serious debate in which there have been serious speeches. I would like to commence, as did the Chief Justice of the Superior Court, in reciting my obligations. I think it is appropriate in this debate to recite precisely what my obligations are, as I see them, to the government and the country. As the Chief Justice in his letter to me recited the Department of Justice Act, so do I. Section 4 states that it is the responsibility of the Minister of Justice, and I quote:
1. to see that the administration of public affairs is in accordance with law, and

2. to have the superintendence of all matters connected with the administration of justice in Canada, not within the jurisdiction of the governments of the provinces.
I have stated in the House and outside the House that in relation to the subject matter the House is debating today and has been for some two weeks, I perceive my duties and responsibilities as being, first, to ensure there is no violation of the laws of Canada, including breaches by the ministers of the Crown and, second, to assist in ensuring the independence and the stature of the judiciary to assure its independence from interference or undue influence.
I agree, as I indicated in the House the other day, with the comments made by the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec on page two of his letter, and I quote:
It is of the utmost importance that this independence of the judiciary, achieved through great effort during the course of the last three centuries, be jealously guarded against all attacks.
More particularly, it must remain protected from interventions from Members of the Cabinet, whatever may be the quality of the intentions that inspire them.
It remains to add, in the light of recent events that it must also be protected from interventions from Parliament.
As I indicated in the House, I subscribe to and support, as any Minister of Justice should and must, that statement by the Chief Justice. He goes on in his letter to me to expand upon his responsibilities toward the defence of his court, the management of his court, and my responsibilities. He states:
There exists then a definite point of contact between your obligations-
He is speaking of my obligations as Minister of Justice.
-and mine, though they may come from different sources.
It was for that reason that he had his responsibilities and I mine and that he considered it his duty to respond to my invitation to comment on the present case.
In outlining the obligations of Minister of Justice I would like to paraphrase Lord Shawcross speaking as Lord Chancellor and quoted in Edwards "The Law Officers of the Crown", which I had to quote to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) the other day when he suggested I was subject to political influence. Lord Shawcross said, and I am paraphrasing, that although the Attorney General is a member of the government he has certain duties which he cannot abdicate in connection with the administration of the law. The Attorney General has to discharge them with complete independence of the government. In these matters the Attorney General's duty, and it is his duty, is to concern himself only with the representation and protection of the public interest.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) spoke this afternoon of cynicism. I quote that expression because it is an expression of the obligations and responsibilities of the Attorney General. They are obligations that I recognize. They are obligations which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and former minister of justice of this country recognize. I raise the matter because I think it is important. If the hon. member for Fundy-Roy-al is talking of cynicism, let there be no cynicism in this House or in this country as to what are the obligations of the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General. These obligations, as I perceive them, and as Lord Shawcross

perceives them, are the same perceptions as the Prime Minister has of the office of the Attorney General.
In this case the public interest as spoken of by the learned Lord Chancellor is to ensure the observance of the law and the independence of the judiciary. This is the course I have pursued since Mr. Justice Mackay first intimated to me allegations of interference with the judiciary by cabinet ministers.
I wish to emphasize, because people have said they do not have the facts, and have made allegations and inuen-dos, that prior to the receipt from Mr. Justice Mackay of specific information which he supplied to me at my request, neither I nor the Deputy Attorney General of Canada had received information from any source concerning these specific allegations or any allegations with respect to interference by ministers with any judges in Canada in connection with matters before them.
I hope members will observe and note that statement carefully and that the gentlemen sitting above you, Mr. Speaker, will note that carefully also.
