Three accusations have been made by the opposition in relation to this matter. The first is that the government is determined to cover up approaches by certain ministers to the judges. The second concerns a so-called double standard in the application of the law about which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) spoke on Friday and again today. The third concerns the alleged interference with the course of justice.
Dealing with the first point, I want to repeat that Mr. Justice Mackay wrote to me on February 9 and that I received his letter on February 11. In that letter the learned judge devoted three lines of a three page letter to a passing reference to interference with the courts by ministers. At that time he provided me with no particulars and no request for any action. My first knowledge of any possible impropriety by ministers vis-a-vis the judiciary was in that letter. My response was sent on February 18. It was a prompt response and it requested further particulars in relation to his very general, passing comment. In his reply on February 20 there was specific reference to three incidents which have given rise to the debate today. He described ministerial conduct as "unwarranted attempts to interfere with the judicial process". I emphasize, however, that even in this letter there was no specific request for action but rather, if one looks at the letter carefully, there is a reference to the end of the exchange of correspondence.
The next thing that happened was this: without being asked by Mr. Justice Mackay to take any action, without
March 16, 1976

any action being suggested to me, I called upon my colleagues for an explanation of the incidents referred to in Mr. Justice Mackay's letter and, as is well known, I wrote to the Chief Justice of the Superior Court on March 4. I thought it proper to write to him because one of the issues which is involved, and one to which members of the opposition paid great attention, is the independence of the judiciary.
I thought it proper to write to the Chief Justice and say to him:
-if there is information indicating that anyone is or has been seeking improperly to interfere with the due administration of justice in a court, by approaches to a judge or otherwise, this is a matter of which the Chief Justice of the Court, as the judge principally responsible for the management of the Court and for protecting its independence and integrity, would be made fully aware.
I am therefore writing to you to invite you to draw to my attention, if you deem such action appropriate, information that may be in your possession respecting any unwarranted attempts to interfere with the proper administration of justice in your Court in respect of matters that should be of concern to me.
There was some question in the House the other day about the use of those words; they were the words used by Mr. Justice Mackay.
I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that my request to the Chief Justice was not limited to the three incidents then in the public domain. I wrote to the Chief Justice, with the concurrence of the Prime Minister, because he is the person principally responsible for the administration and independence of that court. As the Chief Justice says in his letter, the statutory provisions of the Quebec Courts of Justice Act, Section 21(a) and the traditional common law practices which have developed around the office of Chief Justice make it clear that he is the man responsible chiefly for the administration, independence, and integrity of the court.
Next, I wish to emphasize that the Prime Minister, when that letter was sent, agreed immediately, subject to the views of the Chief Justice, to publish the reply upon its receipt. I draw attention to this history because the hon. member for Fundy-Royal spoke at such length this afternoon about the role and the importance of the opposition. The opposition obviously has a role to play, and this is important in a free society. But all these actions were taken by me as Attorney General, with the concurrence of the Prime Minister. The request was made to the Chief Justice, the request was made to Judge Mackay for further particulars, without benefit of questions from the opposition and without pressure from the media of this country.
These things were done on the initiative of myself and of the government to try to determine the facts from the one man in Canada who, under the law, is best able to provide these facts, namely, the Chief Justice of Quebec. I emphasize that they were done without the benefit of pressure from the opposition.

speechtext:
-who made what I would say was a most enlightened and outstandingly good speech this afternoon and set the tone for this debate. I should like to commence my remarks by making reference to one of the points made by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal.
The opposition has been under some criticism because we have dared to ask questions, to which answers have been refused. We have been stonewalled. Even when we got answers a big snow job was done. The Globe and Mail broke the story on March 3, and it was at that time that we met, on what I call that famous Wednesday in parliament, and moved motions and asked questions. I should just like to bring the House up to date on what has happened since that time before I make some further remarks.
We asked for an inquiry but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said there was no need for an inquiry, that nothing was wrong, that there was no influence or intervention. He was the cardinal, he was the pope, he was the queen, and he was the judge of the facts. We have not got those facts even yet. I might direct your attention to the fact that we have yet to receive these facts since the time we asked for an inquiry and the story broke in the Globe and Mail. We have had the letter to which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) referred, written by Mr. Justice Mackay on February 20, and received on February 21. It was not until March 3 that he replied to the letter.
Some other interesting things have happened. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) resigned and then withdrew his resignation because the Prime Minister said he could not do without him. Today we had the resignation of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), now simply the hon. member for Papineau. Without questions, without interrogation, and without a search for that information from the government things of this nature would not have happened.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice talks about a cosy arrangement. The cosy arrangement to which I refer is that arrangement within the executive itself that allows it to create the problems, create the facts, make the decisions, and write the judgments. That is the cosy arrangement.
I do not think we can hide today the facts of the last ten days. Parliament has been shocked, as the country has been shocked. We have been shocked by the action of government ministers in reference to this very serious question of an inquiry into matters concerning the executive power of the judiciary. One resignation today does not
March 16, 1976

solve the issue, and this issue will live in this parliament and with this government for a long time to come.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
It was very interesting to hear the Prime Minister say just a few days ago that there was nothing wrong. He said he had talked to this one and to that one and had sized up the facts and, in his judgment on the facts, nothing was wrong. Today he has set himself adrift, like Robinson Crusoe. He has said now that he has found his ministers were wrong. They did not commit any offence. He has made that decision, it is not one that has been made by anybody else under the criminal code.
The Prime Minister has sized up the facts and says now that his ministers have done wrong things, and that is why he has accepted the resignation of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and that is why he asked for and accepted an apology from the Minister of Public Works. One thing we have learned from the facts today is that the Prime Minister has set himself adrift from the rest of his executive because he felt in his heart, will all his knowledge and his training, that they were in the wrong.
I never thought I would see the day in parliament when the Minister of Public Works, and I agree with some who have said he is a man of high calibre, intelligence, and integrity, would tender his resignation because he had been wrong. The Prime Minister has arrogantly refused to accept that resignation in spite of the serious situation and issue now before the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The issue is not whether judges were influenced. The issue is whether there was an indiscreet attempt by certain ministers to call judges while matters were pending before the courts, and in particular when a member of the executive had been charged and found guilty of contempt of court. This is a very serious matter indeed for any lawyer or any Privy Councillor or member of the executive. It is a very serious matter when such an attempt would be made directly or indirectly by a member of the executive, either thoughtfully or without thought, deliberately or unintentionally.
There apparently was a discussion of a particular matter with the judge. What was that discussion? We have had to pry the facts from the government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
In the earlier days confessions came much easier than now, because the ministers now know they are in serious trouble. On March 3, 1976, I rose in my place and asked the following question:
I will turn, now, to another member of the cabinet, and address a question to the Minister of Public Works. In a letter to the Minister of Justice on February 20, Mr. Justice Mackay stated:
"After Mr. Ouellet asked Mr. John Turner to intervene on his behalf with the judge presiding over the contempt of court proceedings and was promptly rebuffed, he approached Mr. Drury with more success, but, as it turned out, without the desired effect."
Would the Minister of Public Works tell the House whether he was approached and what kind of assistance he rendered?
Alleged Interference with Judiciary
Here is what the minister said:
I may say for the benefit of those who are prepared to listen that in my opinion the integrity, the independence, of the judiciary is critical to the successful running of a country such as ours and I both respect and admire this principle. If it were not for the fact that I consider the Associate Chief Justice of Quebec, whom I have known for a number of years, to be uninfluencible, in a pejorative sense, I would have refrained from intervening-
What has that to do with it, whether he could influence the judge or not? The point I want to emphasize is that an attempt was made, and that is the important issue, not whether the judge is or was influenced. The question is whether there was an attempt directly or indirectly to influence him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Oh, go back to Robinson Crusoe.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The Minister says that he would have refrained from intervening or from having any conversation with him. He said:
Indeed, the only intervention that would be contemplated by me would be one to see that he was in full knowledge of the facts-
Let us stop there. Where does a judge get his facts in conducting any kind of an inquiry or case? He gets those facts from the witnesses called before him, from the records of the court or from documents that have been put in as evidence, and not from the executive or any citizen of Canada. If this is not an attempt to influence a judge, there never has been any attempt.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Then we have the crowning statement that the minister wanted to see that he was in full knowledge of the facts and that he did his duty. I appreciate the prerogative of the Prime Minister in appointing judges, but I do not think the prerogative extends throughout the executive, allowing them to call judges to inform them of their duties or how to perform them. Again I suggest that this is not a question of whether judges were influenced, and I will have something more to say about that, but rather a question involving an attempt by the executive to intervene and to influence a judge. That is the important point.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
I agree with the Minister of Justice and others that we have one of the finest judiciaries in the world. The appointment of judges by all governments has always taken place after a great deal of consideration of a man's education, training, and character, which the bar associations of this country demand of members of the bar. When a person is elevated to the Bench he must accept the challenge. Let me put this by quoting a former judge of the Supreme Court of Canada who was dealing with a commission in respect of a former judge who had resigned, Mr. Landreville. He said:
A study is made of instances in the past where in Great Britain and in the United States the conduct of Judges has been under review by Parliament and by the Courts. The importance of the independence of Judges is emphasized: "It should be the guarantee of security to the weak against the strong and to the individual against the community; it should present a shield against the tyranny of power and arrogance and against the irresponsibility and irrationality of popular action-" "...

Alleged Interference with Judiciary
the underlying basic assumption is the intellectual and moral integrity of the judicial officer in his pronouncements."
We have heard day in and day out that Chief Justice Deschenes has said there was nothing wrong. I am going to refer to his letter, but he never talked to any of these ministers. He did not talk to the former minister of Consumer and corporate affairs or to the Minister of Public Works, and he did not talk to The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). He has talked to his judges, and all he has said is that his judges have exonerated themselves and have done nothing wrong. But he has not had the chance to talk to the minister. I am glad the Minister of Justice has returned.
The Chief Justice has not talked to the ministers. How could he find, in view of the fact that he had no evidence before him, that the ministers had done no wrong? The only person marking that decision is the Prime Minister. He said they had done no wrong. That is why we are continually asking and that is why we have this motion before us, for which I congratulate the NDP, asking for an inquiry. The people of Canada and members of parliament are entitled to the facts, and those facts have not been obtained. They have been given to a judge secretly and quietly, The Prime Minister says he is the judge. He is the cardinal, he is the pope, he is the queen, he is everything. He has made the decision, he is judge and jury.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
On the admission of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) there should have been a public inquiry, the kind of inquiry established by law so that information could be bared and so that we could have it before parliament and before the Canadian people. That is what we are requesting.
I know, Mr. Speaker, they have watched this for ten days and they cannot back out of it. They have even used questions of privilege which are fraudulent. They have used every method to avoid answering questions. Yet the Prime Minister, who must take the responsibility for it, says there is nothing wrong. I think there is something wrong "in the state of Denmark", there is something wrong with the executive and something wrong with this government.
What are the facts? This is what the Minister of Justice said, and these are the only facts we know, the ones we pried out of the government. The former minister of consumer and corporate affairs was charged and found guilty of contempt of court because he ridiculed Justice Mackay's decision on the sugar case. He used such words-here I paraphrase-as that a judge that would make that decision would have to be insane.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Silly decision.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
That shows just how arrogant the Liberals still are.
The former minister of consumer and corporate affairs sought advice from the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, who refused to intervene or interfere, who in fact rebuffed the minister. Then he turned to the Minister of Public Works, a lawyer, a Queen's counsel, a distinguished

soldier, a minister of the Crown, who placed a call to Mr. Justice Hugessen. He called the judge to give him some facts and to tell him what his duties were.
What did Chief Justice Deschenes say in his report? His examination and his research were in reference to judges. He found their conduct above reproach, but he set out very clearly that he had no mandate in law or in ethics to examine what parliament was doing or what the ministers of the Crown were doing, or what members of parliament were doing. There is the issue, there is the essence of the indictments against the Prime Minister and his government and his failure to tell parliament and the people of Canada what his ministers are up to and why they feel they have the God given right, because the Prime Minister appointed them to the executive, to breach all the rules of the bar association, and indeed breach the ethics and standards of the very essence of democracy, the foundations of which rest upon a complete separation of the powers of the executive and the judiciary.
Let us take a look at what Chief Justice Deschenes said. He reminded the Liberal government of one of its great leaders, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He said:
It is a strange doctrine to preach that the judges are responsible to parliament. Where is that responsibility? I have always understood that the judges were responsible only to their own conscience, and parliament has no power over them. True, they can be removed, but only on an address of both Houses of parliament. That law has been adopted to make them absolutely independent of parliament, and they are only responsible to parliament in extreme cases of malfeasance.
He also said:
It seems to me that we must discard any suggestion that the Canadian Judicial Council has a role to play in this matter. Its jurisdiction relates to an examination of complaints relating to the conduct of judges and not to complaints that might concern the conduct of third parties in relation to them
-namely, ministers who intervene, who call judges and try to tell them what their duties are. That is what Mr. Justice Deschenes told them.
He also said this:
I consider myself however under no obligation in relation to Parliament-save that of good behaviour-nor towards the government, and the invitations to undertake an inquiry which have been addressed to me in the House of Commons appear to me to be out of place.
In other words, he said it would probably be out of place for him to make any comment on what the ministers did or what the members of parliament did in their intervention or in their attempt to influence judges. That letter of the Chief Justice has no bearing on the issue in finding out what went on within the executive and how they attempted to influence judges.
The Chief Justice also said:
I was not appointed to conduct a commission of inquiry and of course it is obviously not one of my functions to set myself up as a semi-official investigator on behalf of the House of Commons.
Then he went on to talk about what happened with reference to the telephone conversation with the Minister of Public Works and he gave an account of what Justice Hugessen wrote to him on the subject as follows:
Mr. Drury telephoned me during the hearing of the contempt proceedings against Andre Ouellet. The call came to my home, in the evening, after dinner, when I was in the basement helping my youngest son...
March 16, 1976

Then he went on the say what the minister said to him. When the Prime Minister said there had been no offences under the code, perhaps someone should take a look at the code. This is what Mr. Justice Hugessen wrote:
The conversation dealt with two aspects of the Ouellet case:
1. Whether it would be possible for Mr. Ouellet to make a formal apology-

speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with deep regret that we on this side of the House have heard that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) had chosen to tender his resignation as minister.
As a result of the controversy and the extent of politiza-tion brought in this issue, it had become impossible for him to discharge his responsibilities as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and to continue to protect the interests of the Canadian consumers.
During the brief period in which I had the pleasure to sit with him in the House, I was often impressed by his ability, the respect he was showing for his responsibilities and his warm relations with backbenchers.
His departure from the cabinet will be a serious loss for the government. However, we hope that one day in the near future he will be re-appointed as a minister.

No one can have sat in this Chamber or read the debates concerning this matter without being conscious of the strong feelings held on both sides of the House. No need exists for me to recite the facts. Certainly the motion as proposed by the NDP is extreme in its critical implications, in my judgment unduly so.
For whatever reason, we are now engrossed in what is at worst an unseemly squabble, at best an assurance that direct ministerial communications to judges on cases being considered by them will be a thing of the past.
In respect of the controversy I would wish to deal with the independence of the judiciary, the call for a public inquiry, and the related situation of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury).
The independence of the judiciary of this country as guaranteed by law and tradition is inviolate. This is underlined by the quotation of a speech by Sir Wilfrid Laurier to this House on September 15, 1903, as quoted by Chief Justice Deschenes in his report. The only power parliament itself has over judges is to remove them on grounds of malfeasance, but only on an address of both Houses of Parliament.
Clearly, then, if Parliament itself lacks any power over the judiciary, no member of parliament or single minister
Alleged Interference with Judiciary could be in such a position. Cries by opposition members that the judiciary is a fragile blossom which might be trampled on by a minister, no matter how powerful, are sheer nonsense. The judiciary is independent and will remain so, not because of the forbearance of the government but because it has guaranteed rights which cannot be thwarted by parliament itself.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The question of a public inquiry opens problems for parliament and the judiciary which seem to me to be difficult in the extreme. Since parliament should zealously guard its privileges, any such inquiry involving its own members or members of the judiciary should necessarily be by a committee of parliament. If the misdemeanour lies with a judge, that is a parliamentary responsibility. If the misdemeanour is that of a member of parliament or minister responsible to parliament, that matter also must be heard by parliament.
Clearly, parliament would not wish to delegate this fundamental task to an outside body. We might thus have a committee of parliament conducting an inquisitorial investigation of what ministers might have said to ministers, what ministers might have said to judges, what judges might have said to judges, what judges might have said to lawyers, what lawyers acting for judges might have said to newspaper reporters, and so on, and on, and on. Even if parliament were to delegate the function to an outside appointed tribunal of inquiry, the same features would exist. Surely those wishing to maintain public respect for the independence of the judiciary would not welcome such a form of inquisition.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: They would not phone a judge either.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
The report of the Chief Justice of Quebec recited the facts and concluded that no impropriety could be asserted to have been committed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) or the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). Nonetheless, they both apologized for any possible embarrassment caused by their contacts with the justices in question. Chief Justice Deschenes characterized the phone call of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) as grave, presumably meaning serious, or even very serious. Justice Hugessen had himself thought the call improper and so advised the minister at the time of the call.
There is now no doubt in anyone's mind that the phone conversation should not have taken place. The minister has recognized the impropriety of the act by an apology and by the tendering of his resignation. The question is, then, of the consequences or the penalty. The minister, with his unquestioned sense of public responsibility, saw his duty and carried it out. He was entirely prepared to accept the extreme penalty of climaxing a brilliant and honourable career by an exit in disgrace. Surely even the most uncharitable would look at all the facts and question the severity of the sentence which would be imposed if the minister's tendered resignation were accepted.
First, with regard to the telephone conversation itself, forgetting for a moment the indiscretion in placing the call, Mr. Justice Hugessen reported two items. One was to ask if an apology could bring the proceedings to an end.

March 16, 1976
Alleged Interference with Judiciary The other was to advise of a situation the minister perceived respecting English-speaking, French-speaking relations.
Again, setting aside the question of the act of telephoning the judge, the minister believed he was conversing on a personal level with the best intentions in mind. I have heard no one assert anything to the contrary, and certainly not Mr. Justice Hugessen.
The facts of the indiscretion, coupled with the comments of the Chief Justice, presented the minister with the only honourable course to which he felt he had recourse, that is, to offer a full apology and his resignation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) quite properly, in my judgment, brought other tests to bear. He acknowledged the lapse of judgment; he did not excuse it. He recognized that in future, with the present example in mind, that a harsher penalty might be applied. He also recognized that the career of one of the most dedicated, honourable public servants produced by this country should not be destroyed by this single lapse of judgment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
In the relatively unchartered waters presented by such a case it is difficult to know what sort of penalty should fall on a minister. It is an unsolved problem of democracy as to what penalty should follow from errors, follies, ignorance or even innocent miscalculations. In sterner times heads were the forfeit.
Despite willingness to acknowledge the splendid record of the Minister of Public Works, his integrity, and the basically innocent motivation behind his impropriety, some hon. members now seek his head, figuratively, as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: We want your head.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Well, you won't get it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Surely the motivation behind an indiscretion or impropriety of this sort must be considered. If it was greed, venality, or even a desire to enhance his personal power, it could be understood and condemned. In this case, knowing the man, knowing what he said, and knowing his high standards of personal integrity, his motive was an honest desire to help a friend and a colleague.
In any event, the error was made. Perhaps one should recall the disarming remark of that great President of the United States, Franklin Roosevelt.

speechtext:
Franklin Roosevelt said, "I don't often make a mistake, but when I do it's a lulu."
In recent days we have heard the comparison made with the incident involving Hugh Dalton, British Chancellor of the Exchequer, who was obliged to resign when a newspa-

per printed a budget item which was leaked. In that case, though the indiscretion did not result in any action detrimental to the state, there was the long principle of the inviolability of the budget and the discretion of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. In the letter Prime Minister Atlee wrote accepting Dalton's resignation he pointed out this specific feature of the circumstance, and the historic character.
In this case before our parliament there was neither an attempt to influence the judge, as confirmed by the judge, not a feasible ability to do so. Nor again was there the long, hallowed tradition of a budget indiscretion. The analogy breaks down on every count.
I do not take issue with the oppostion criticism of the government's embarrassment in this issue. Not only is the government vulnerable, but I think the principle of judicial independence has been reinforced.
I do not support the idea of a public inquiry, for the reasons I have cited.
The core of my plea is a simple one. It is that all of us recognize that too few men of the character of the Minister of Public Works have given their lives to the public service of this country. His career has been a noble one in the highest possible tradition. Whatever else might come of this sorry chapter, I plead with the House to recognize that sometimes, in the words of the poet, "mercy should allay our stern resentment".
In a few days or weeks the House presumably will have turned its attention to other matters. I hope, and indeed pray that the honourable career of the Minister of Public Works will not be a tragic and unnecessary casualty of battle.

Yes, I have lost my notes, solely and simply because I was not prepared to get into this until the Minister of Justice spoke. He made a great thing of saying that he received a letter on February 11 of this year from Mr. Justice Mackay which contained several broad allegations of improper activity on the part of his fellow ministers.
He did not act immediately on those allegations by letter. Instead he waited seven full days until February 18, one full week, until February 18 before he then fired off a letter to Mr. Justice Mackay which in effect said to Mr. Justice Mackay: what do you mean?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext: It was pretty obvious what he meant.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED INTERFERENCE WITH JUDICIAL PROCESS BY SOME MINISTERS
speechtext:
I think one week is far too long for a minister of justice to delay on a matter as important as that. In any event, on February 18 he dated a letter to Mr. Justice Mackay and said "I want details, I want specifics, I want the actual facts; no more of these allegations because I do not know."
Mr. Justice Mackay got that letter on February 19 and on February 20 dated a letter to the Minister of Justice in which he indicated in some detail fairly specific allegations of improper activity on the part of three of the colleagues of the Minister of Justice in the ministry respecting interference, or respecting intervention in any event, with members of the judiciary in the province of Quebec. On February 20 that letter was dispatched by Mr. Justice Mackay. The minister has not indicated when it reached his office but I suspect that was at least on February 21.
The minister comes along in a great blaze of glory here tonight to say that, under no pressure from anyone, on March 4 he sent off an epistle to Chief Justice Deschenes asking him to investigate the whole matter.
May I merely point out to you. Sir, that on the evening of March 2, fully two days before that letter of March 4 to Chief Justice Mackay, this story broke in the press of this country. The Globe and Mail on the evening of March 2 broke the story.

In any event, I merely want to say that, to me, the Minister of Justice was derelict in his duty by sitting or having others in his office sit on that letter between February 21 and March 4 before he did anything about it.

I think as well that the Minister of Justice, after giving us a lecture on the duties of attorneys general in this country, also did the wrong thing when he had that information. He referred it to a chief justice-a well renowned chief justice of this country, in such an odd way. I do not know if such a reference has ever been made before by a minister of justice in this country relating to a matter of such importance to a member of the judiciary, for that member of the judiciary to act in any manner, shape or form.
I merely want to read to you, sir, two short paragraphs from Chief Justice Deschenes' report which are selfexplanatory. To me they are a very sharp rap over the knuckles to the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). On page 4 of the report Chief Justice Deschenes said:
I consider myself however under no obligation in relation to parliament-save that of good behaviour-nor towards the government, and the invitations to undertake an inquiry which have been addressed to me in the House of Commons appear to me to be out of place.
All I can say to the Minister of Justice in relation to that is "hear, hear" for Chief Justice Deschenes because it was a wrong proposal in the first place not to give the man the investigative machinery or equipment he needed. This was a report that had to be based on an investigation when the Chief Justice really had one hand tied behind his back. He also said:
I can also only dismiss the proposition that I proceed to interview privately one or other members of the cabinet whose names were mentioned in the House. I was not appointed to conduct a commission of inquiry and of course it is obviously not one of my functions to set myself up as a semi-official investigator on behalf of the House of Commons.
Sir, no complete, thorough, impartial investigation could be made by Chief Justice Deschenes under those halfhearted terms of reference given to him by the Minister of Justice who boasts tonight about his separate and impartial duties.
I say that the Minister of Justice was derelict in his duty by doing what he did: he is still, sitting there tonight, derelict in his duty because he will not call, whether his Prime Minister likes or not-because he as Attorney General of Canada will not call a public judicial inquiry into this matter.

speechtext:
Why, I have known of ministers of finance being bounced out of office simply because they revealed some contents of a budget minutes before the budget speech was made in the House. That was not illegal, but it was improper. Traditionally, under our British parliamentary system of government, such improper actions are enough to force a minister's resignation.
This afternoon we heard the Prime Minister lecture us on what could be done in a contempt of court action. I could not believe my ears when I listened to him. Let me repeat at least one sentence of his speech, and if I misquote I hope the right hon. gentleman will say so. Talking about the intervention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) with associate Chief Justice Hugessen, the Prime Minister said this afternoon, and I quote, "It was important to know in some way what sort of an apology would be expected," He was referring to the apology to be made to Mr. Justice Mackay. Mr. Speaker, bargaining like that, on the part of a party to an action or others, should take place in court, preferably in open court, in the presence of counsel for both parties.
That a minister of the Crown, who himself is a member of the bar should do something expressly forbidden by the code of ethics of the province in which he was called to the

bar makes the offence more heinous. He did something which ought not to be done in any circumstances. I do not care what his motives were. The very fact he intervened with a justice seized of the matter is enough.
Again this matter came to our knowledge not because any minister was impelled, on the grounds of political morality, to disclose anything. We know about it because a member of the Quebec bar blew the whistle on the government. A disgruntled lawyer had not received his fees, and that led to disclosure. That is why the judge himself felt impelled to write the letter. Unless there is a public inquiry the public of this country will wonder on how many other occasions such an intervention took place.
Only after these matters were made public did something else happen. Forced by the media, by what took place on the floor of the House of Commons and by public opinion, the Minister of Public Works tendered his resignation. His delay in tendering it should be remembered.
The final act occurred today when the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs tendered his resignation. His excuse for tendering it was that somehow the contempt of court appeal hanging over his head made him unable to perform his duties as a responsible minister of the Crown. Sir, tonight we are in the third week of March, 1976. The former minister's notice of appeal was filed in the last week of January, 1976. If the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs was truly upset by this sword hanging over his head, why did he wait until this late hour before resigning?
I think the Prime Minister was derelict in his duty in not asking for, and receiving, specific information on this matter. He ought to have received it long ago. I think the Minister of Public Works was derelict in not submitting his resignation long ago. The Minister of Justice was also derelict in his delays. I condemn the former principal aide to the Prime Minister for delaying disclosure of the part he played in this matter. There is one reason and one reason only for these delays. The information has to be dragged out of these ministers on the floor of the House of Commons. If it were not for the work of the media we might know nothing of this. Faced with the criticism in the House and in the media, they grudgingly did something which ought to have been done weeks ago. In the case of two ministers it ought to have been done years ago.
Only one course of action will satisfy the members of this House. Hon. members, including those of the Prime Minister's party, know that only a full, complete, public and impartial judicial inquiry into this whole sorry mess of wire pulling and influence pushing will satisfy the people of this country.
